appetite.statement: The board accepts risk in pursuit of Nimbus's growth, but not evenly. We hold a low appetite for any loss of confidentiality of customer data and for any AI output that misstates our policies or our commitments to customers. We hold a moderate appetite for availability incidents that are resolved within one hour, provided customers are kept informed through the status page. We hold zero appetite for non-compliance that would forfeit the Texas SB 2610 safe harbor or the affirmative defense under the Texas Responsible AI Governance Act, because both protections depend on continuous maintenance rather than a one-time effort. Any risk whose residual score sits above the appetite line is reported to the board each quarter with a treatment decision.
appetite.plain: Leadership has written down how much risk is acceptable. Losing customer data or letting an AI assistant misstate a policy is not acceptable, a short outage is tolerable, and losing the legal protections Texas offers is never acceptable.
appetite.scale: likelihood 1 to 5 times impact 1 to 5; appetite line at 9

risks.title: Credential compromise of an administrator leads to a customer data breach
risks.plain: An attacker steals an administrator's login and uses it to read or copy customer data.
risks.scenario: A phishing message or malware on a laptop captures an administrator's password and session. With that access the attacker reaches the production console, exports customer account data, and the exposure starts notification clocks in Texas, in the EU, and under customer contracts. Phishing-resistant second factors, prompt removal of access, and centralized logs are the main brakes.
risks.treatment_note: Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication on every administrator account, quarterly access reviews, and centralized logging. Residual impact stays at 5 because a successful compromise still exposes regulated data; the annual loss scenario (S-01) puts a dollar range on it.
risks.kri: Administrator accounts without phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (target 0); leaver access removed within one business day (target 100 percent)

risks.title: Prompt injection through a conversation or pasted text makes an AI assistant leak data or misstate policy
risks.plain: Someone types or pastes text that tricks an AI assistant into ignoring its rules, so it reveals something it should not or states a policy that does not exist.
risks.scenario: A visitor pastes a block of text that carries hidden instructions, or a knowledge-base edit for the session carries them. The assistant treats the text as orders rather than data and answers with an invented refund policy or repeats content from its own instructions. Because transcripts are never stored the harm is bounded to that session, but a screenshot of a false policy can still reach a customer.
risks.treatment_note: Visitor text is capped and labelled untrusted, model output is validated against an allow-list, and every finding from adversarial testing gets a gate that prevents regression. The attack class keeps evolving, so residual likelihood stays at 3 and the risk remains above the appetite line; it is reported to the board each quarter.
risks.kri: Injection test cases passing in the endpoint gate (target: all); new adversarial findings per quarter

risks.title: Abuse of public AI endpoints drives runaway model spend or degraded service
risks.plain: Because anyone on the internet can talk to the assistants, a script could hammer them and run up the model bill or slow the service for real visitors.
risks.scenario: A bot or a curious visitor sends thousands of chat requests in minutes. Each request costs money at the model provider and occupies server capacity, so without limits the monthly bill could multiply overnight while genuine visitors see errors. This has been observed on the live assistants: a per-visitor rate limit and a daily cap were added after abuse concerns, and the limiter is per warm instance rather than global.
risks.treatment_note: Per-visitor rate limit, daily cap, input length caps, and a kill switch bound the spend. Known limit: the limiter is per warm serverless instance; a shared store would make it global and is on the backlog.
risks.kri: Model spend per day against the daily cap; rate-limited (429) responses per day

risks.title: Known vulnerability in a dependency exploited on a public surface
risks.plain: A code library the site uses has a publicly known flaw, and someone uses it before the fix is applied.
risks.scenario: A vulnerability is published for a library in the build or runtime chain. The daily audit flags it, but if the fix is not applied inside the remediation window an attacker can use the published exploit against a public endpoint. The trust center and the assistants keep runtime dependencies at zero, which shrinks this surface to build-time tools.
risks.treatment_note: Lockfile pinning, a daily dependency audit, remediation windows by severity, and gates that block deployment when a check fails.
risks.kri: Open critical or high dependency findings past their remediation window (target 0)

risks.title: Model vendor changes model behavior without notice
risks.plain: The company that provides the AI model can change how it behaves, so the assistants could start answering differently with no change on our side.
risks.scenario: The provider retires a model version or changes a default. This has happened: a model upgrade on the Nimbus assistants began billing hidden reasoning tokens against the reply budget and truncated answers mid-sentence until the configuration was corrected. Pinned model names and a full regression run after every change are the safeguards; residual likelihood stays high because the change is outside Nimbus's control.
risks.treatment_note: Model names are pinned by environment variable and the full test matrix runs after any change. Decision required from the board: fund the qualification of a second model provider behind the same configuration switch (estimated two engineer-weeks plus an ongoing evaluation cost), or formally accept single-vendor concentration for the next 12 months.
risks.kri: Days since the last full regression run against the pinned model; unplanned model behavior changes detected per quarter

risks.title: Hosting or model provider outage makes the product or assistants unavailable
risks.plain: If the hosting company or the AI provider goes down, customers cannot reach the product or the assistants until the provider recovers.
risks.scenario: A regional outage at the hosting provider or an incident at the model provider takes the assistants offline or slows the product. Nimbus cannot fix the provider; it can only detect quickly, show an honest unavailable state, and keep customers informed through the status page. Most provider incidents resolve within an hour, which is inside the board's moderate appetite for short availability incidents.
risks.treatment_note: Accepted within the availability appetite: provider status feeds are monitored, the health probe switches the status pill off, and provider service credits apply. A second hosting region or provider was judged not worth the cost at 180 employees; revisit if the number of customers on the Enterprise uptime commitment grows.
risks.kri: Monthly availability of the product and of the assistants' health endpoint (target 99.9 percent); provider incidents affecting Nimbus per quarter

risks.title: SB 2610 safe harbor lost because framework maintenance lapses
risks.plain: Texas protects companies that keep following a recognized security framework. If Nimbus lets its program go stale, that protection disappears exactly when it would be needed, after a breach.
risks.scenario: The safe harbor requires that the framework be adopted and maintained, including keeping up with revisions. If reviews are skipped, evidence goes stale, or a framework revision is ignored, a plaintiff after a breach can argue the program was not maintained and seek exemplary damages. The daily evidence job and the annual adoption memo exist to make maintenance visible and dated.
risks.treatment_note: Zero appetite. The adoption memo, the quarterly register review, the annual policy review, exception expiry, and the daily evidence bundle each produce dated proof that the program is being maintained.
risks.kri: Stale or failing checks in the daily evidence bundle (target 0); days since the framework adoption memo was reviewed (target under 365)

risks.title: An AI system is deployed without inventory, oversight, or NIST AI RMF alignment, weakening the TRAIGA defense
risks.plain: If a team launches an AI feature without listing it and setting rules for it, Nimbus loses the legal defense Texas gives to companies that follow the national AI risk framework.
risks.scenario: A product team ships an AI feature or an internal agent quickly, without adding it to the inventory, naming an owner, or defining what it may do. If that system later harms someone, Nimbus cannot show the Attorney General that it followed the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and the affirmative defense under the Texas Responsible AI Governance Act is weakened. The build fails when an inventory entry is incomplete, which catches systems that are listed but not the ones that are missing.
risks.treatment_note: The AI use policy requires approval before launch, the inventory is the control, and every entry needs an owner, allowed actions, human oversight, logging, and a kill switch before the build passes.
risks.kri: AI inventory entries with every required field and a review within 180 days (target 100 percent); AI features found in release notes but missing from the inventory (target 0)

risks.title: Shadow AI: staff paste customer data into unapproved AI tools
risks.plain: An employee pastes a customer's data into an AI app the company has not checked, and that data is now somewhere Nimbus does not control.
risks.scenario: A support agent or an analyst pastes a customer ticket, an export, or a contract into a consumer AI tool to save time. The tool may retain the text or use it for training, and Nimbus has no contract with its provider. Discovery is quarterly through expense and browser-extension reviews, so a leak could go unnoticed for up to three months, which is why this risk sits above the appetite line.
risks.treatment_note: Policy, training, an approved tool list, and quarterly discovery are in place; continuous discovery is not (exception EX-03). Decision required from the board: fund a software discovery and data-loss-prevention subscription for continuous monitoring, or extend the quarterly review when EX-03 expires and accept the residual exposure.
risks.kri: Unapproved AI services found in the quarterly expense and software discovery review (target 0); staff trained on the AI use policy (target 100 percent)

risks.title: A breach notification deadline is missed
risks.plain: After a data breach, the law and customer contracts set strict clocks for telling people. Missing one turns a bad incident into a legal problem.
risks.scenario: A breach is confirmed late on a Friday. The 72-hour EU clock, the Texas 60-day and 30-day windows, the healthcare business associate terms, and customer contract windows all start at different moments. If triage is slow or a vendor's own breach notice arrives late, the notification procedure cannot be executed in time.
risks.treatment_note: Written declaration criteria, four-hour triage, and a procedure that lists every clock and its owner. Vendor notice windows are the weak link; one vendor contract is missing the clause (exception EX-01).
risks.kri: Time from incident declaration to a completed legal duty assessment (target under 24 hours), measured in tabletop exercises and real incidents

risks.title: Backup failure discovered only during a restore
risks.plain: The backups look fine until the day they are needed, and then they do not work.
risks.scenario: A silent change to a database layout, an expired credential on the backup job, or an untested retention setting leaves the backups incomplete. Nobody notices until an incident forces a restore, at which point customer data is lost or recovery takes days instead of hours.
risks.treatment_note: Daily automated backups to an isolated location with integrity checks, and a quarterly restore test that is recorded with a sign-off.
risks.kri: Days since the last successful restore test (target 90 or fewer); backup job failures per month (target 0)

risks.title: Over-permissioned or leaked service credential or API key
risks.plain: Software and AI systems log in with their own keys. If one leaks or can do more than it needs, an outsider can use it as if they were the system.
risks.scenario: The model key or a cloud service credential is committed to the repository, printed in a log, or scoped far wider than its job. Someone finds it and uses it to run up spend or reach data. The model key is a standing key rotated by hand rather than a short-lived identity, which is recorded as an exception.
risks.treatment_note: Secrets live only in platform environment variables, the repository is secret-scanned on every build and daily, and non-human identities are inventoried and rotated. Target state is a short-lived workload identity for the model key (exception EX-02).
risks.kri: Secret scan failures per month (target 0); non-human credentials past their 180-day rotation date (target 0)

risks.title: A customer security questionnaire is answered inaccurately
risks.plain: An answer sent to a customer says Nimbus does something it does not do, which can become a broken promise in a contract later.
risks.scenario: Under deadline pressure, a questionnaire answer is copied from an older submission or written from memory. It claims a control that is only partial, or leaves out an open exception. If the customer later relies on that answer in a contract or an audit, the inaccuracy becomes a misrepresentation.
risks.treatment_note: Every answer must cite a control ID and current evidence from this trust center; partial controls and open exceptions are answered as such; the Security Lead reviews before submission.
risks.kri: Questionnaire answers traced to a control ID and evidence (target 100 percent); corrections issued after submission (target 0)

risks.title: Ransomware through a workforce device
risks.plain: A staff laptop gets infected, and the infection spreads or locks up files the company needs.
risks.scenario: A staff member opens a malicious attachment on a company laptop. The malware encrypts local files and tries to reach shared drives and production. Managed endpoint protection and the rule that unmanaged devices cannot reach production limit the spread; isolated backups make the ransom demand irrelevant for data recovery.
risks.treatment_note: Endpoint protection, awareness training, alerting, and isolated backups reduce the likelihood and the recovery time; the remaining financial exposure (response costs and business interruption) is transferred to a cyber insurance policy (simulated) that includes ransomware cover.
risks.kri: Managed device coverage (target 100 percent); devices with anti-malware updates more than 7 days overdue (target 0)

risks.title: An AI assistant gives harmful, discriminatory, or policy-violating output to a customer
risks.plain: One of the assistants says something offensive, unfair, or against Nimbus policy to a real person.
risks.scenario: A customer asks an edge-case question and the model produces an answer that is demeaning, that treats people differently because of a protected characteristic, or that invents a discount or a refund. The person is harmed or misled, and under the Texas AI law and the EU AI Act the company must show it had oversight, testing, and a way to switch the system off.
risks.treatment_note: Grounded answers with citations, persona rules checked at build, adversarial testing before release and after model changes, a kill switch, and an AI incident escalation path with a one-hour internal notification.
risks.kri: Harmful-output findings open in the register (target 0); hand-off and refusal rates from session metrics reviewed monthly for drift
